title: A practical guide to Postgres indexes
paragraphs: If a query on a large table feels slow, the cause is usually that Postgres is reading every row to find the few you asked for. An index is a separate data structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, the way the index at the back of a book lets you find a topic without reading every page. This tutorial walks through the index types you will meet most often, how to create them, and how to check that a query is actually using them.

Start with the default: the B-tree index. Running CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id) builds a balanced tree of the values in that column. A B-tree handles equality (customer_id = 42), ranges (created_at between two dates), sorting (ORDER BY created_at) and prefix matches on text. It is the right choice for most columns, and it is what Postgres builds for primary keys and unique constraints automatically.

Before adding an index, look at the plan. Prefix a query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and read the output from the innermost node outward. A Seq Scan means Postgres read the whole table. An Index Scan or Index Only Scan means it used an index. Compare the estimated rows with the actual rows: a large gap usually means the table statistics are stale, and running ANALYZE on the table refreshes them. Never guess; the plan tells you where the time went.

Indexes can cover more than one column. A multicolumn index on (customer_id, created_at) serves queries that filter on customer_id alone, and queries that filter on both columns, but it does not help a query that filters only on created_at. Column order matters: put the column you compare with equality first, and the one you use for ranges or sorting second. A good rule is to design the index from the WHERE clause of your most frequent query.

A partial index stores entries only for rows that match a condition. If ninety percent of your orders are already shipped and your application only ever searches for the unshipped ones, CREATE INDEX orders_open_idx ON orders (created_at) WHERE shipped_at IS NULL is far smaller and faster to maintain than a full index. The query must repeat the same condition in its WHERE clause for Postgres to consider the partial index.

An index on an expression helps when you search on a computed value. If your application looks up users by lowercased email, an ordinary index on email will not be used for WHERE lower(email) = 'ada@example.com'. Create the index on lower(email) instead, and the planner will use it. The same idea works for dates truncated to the day or for fields pulled out of a JSON document.

Not every column fits a B-tree. For arrays, JSONB documents and full-text search, use a GIN index, which maps each element or word to the rows that contain it. For very large tables that are naturally ordered, such as append-only event logs, a BRIN index stores only the minimum and maximum value of each block of pages, and is tiny compared with a B-tree. Pick the type from the query, not from habit.

Indexes are not free. Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE has to update each index on the table, so a table with ten indexes writes roughly ten times as much. Indexes also take disk space and memory. Check which ones are used with the pg_stat_user_indexes view: an index whose idx_scan count stays at zero for weeks is a candidate for removal. Drop unused indexes carefully, and test on a copy first.

On a busy production table, build indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. The ordinary form blocks writes to the table while it runs, which can mean an outage for a large table. The concurrent form takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction block, but it lets your application keep writing. If it fails it leaves an invalid index behind, which you should drop and recreate.

Common mistakes are worth listing. Indexing every column just in case; indexing a column with only two or three distinct values, where a scan is often cheaper; wrapping an indexed column in a function so the index cannot be used; and forgetting that a LIKE pattern starting with a percent sign cannot use a B-tree. Each of these shows up quickly if you read the query plan before and after the change.

To summarize the workflow: find the slow query, read its EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, add the narrowest index that matches its WHERE and ORDER BY clauses, run the query again, and confirm the plan changed and the time dropped. Then watch the index usage statistics over the next few weeks. Treat indexes as a tool you tune with evidence, not a switch you flip once.
